meta.tagline: La Concha's golden sand and the world's finest standing-up cuisine

pills: The pintxo capital of the world
La Concha — Europe's most elegant beach
Among the most Michelin stars per capita

overview.title: Welcome to San Sebastián
overview.intro: San Sebastián — Donostia in Basque — shone as a royal beach resort and was crowned as a culinary empire. La Concha's oyster-shell bay curves with belle époque grace, while the old town behind it hides the densest delicious square metres on earth: bar counters armed with pintxos, a different speciality behind every door. Here food is not a hobby but an identity — the gastronomic societies are a century old, and arguments are conducted in recipes. A beach towel and an appetite: this city's two admission tickets.

local_word.definition: The ritual of drifting from bar to bar with small glasses and pintxos: the backbone of Basque social life. The rule is simple — one pintxo and one small drink per bar, then walk. No sitting, no loyalty, only discovery.

rules.title: Never settle in one pintxo bar
rules.description: Every bar has one champion pintxo, and a local eats only that thing in each: tortilla in one, txuleta in another, idiazabal in a third. Whoever fills up at a single bar fails the city's exam — wander, choose, move on.

rules.title: Learn the counter's rules
rules.description: The cold pintxos sit on the counter, but the real gems are on the hot list: order from the board on the wall. Napkins are dropped on the floor — a littered floor isn't rude, it's a good bar's badge. The bill works on honest declaration at the exit; don't break the trust system.

rules.title: Pour txakoli from a height, don't miss cider season
rules.description: The lightly sparkling white txakoli is poured from high up to aerate it — not showmanship, technique. From January to April the cider houses (sagardotegi) open: cider from the barrel at the cry of 'txotx', with the ritual omelette and txuleta alongside.

quick_facts.label: Getting around
quick_facts.sub: Beach promenade + old town, all flat

tip.label: The Donostia philosophy
tip.text: In this city eating fast is as rude as sitting indoors on a sunny day: a pintxo crawl never takes less than two hours, and the evening paseo is walked on La Concha. Be generous with your stomach and your clock — the city repays it with interest.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Donostia is compact and flat: the beaches, the old town and Gros link up on foot; a funicular for the hills and a bus for the surroundings suffice.

items.title: From the airports
items.description: The city's small airport (EAS) is 20 minutes away; most international flights land at Bilbao (BIO) — from there a direct bus reaches the station in an hour and a quarter. Biarritz (BIQ) is the third option.

items.title: On foot along the promenade
items.description: An unbroken seafront walk from Zurriola to La Concha and on to Ondarreta: the city's main transport axis is the beach railing. The white-balustraded promenade is the official track of the evening paseo.

items.title: The city buses (Dbus)
items.description: A clean network for the hill neighbourhoods and the Miramón side: board with a contactless card. Rarely needed on the tourist route — this is a walking city.

items.title: The Igueldo funicular
items.description: Wooden carriages running since 1912 climb Monte Igueldo: at the top, a nostalgic funfair and the city's most famous view — La Concha's exact postcard angle.

items.title: Basque escapes
items.description: Hondarribia by bus in 40 minutes, the Getaria-Zarautz coast in half an hour, Bilbao and the Guggenheim in an hour and a quarter: Donostia is the perfect base for the Basque coast. The Topo train even crosses the border into France.

callout.label: View tip
callout.text: Take the funicular up Igueldo but climb Urgull on foot: two hills, two different angles. Urgull is free, and from the ramparts beneath the statue the old town + bay view turns gold at sunset.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Donostia distances are short and the differences in character sharp: the old town's noisy heart, Centro's elegance, Gros's surfer ease.

local_word.definition: Txikiteo's glass-focused sibling: roaming bar to bar with friends over small wines (potes). The official reason the streets fill on Friday evenings — the hubbub isn't noise, it's the city's pulse.

items.name: Parte Vieja (the Old Town)
items.description: Streets with a world-record density of bars: step out the door, land at a counter. Night noise is part of the bargain — come with earplugs and descend with an appetite.

items.name: Centro (Área Romántica)
items.description: Belle époque façades, the cathedral quarter and two steps to La Concha: shopping, pastry shops and quiet nights. The address of classic Donostia comfort.

items.name: Gros
items.description: The surfer quarter of Zurriola beach: third-wave coffee, young pintxo bars and a beach rhythm. Five minutes to the old town over the bridge — the warmest dose of local life.

items.name: Antiguo and Ondarreta
items.description: The settled neighbourhood behind Ondarreta beach: a family beach, tennis-club calm and the foot of Igueldo. Twenty minutes to the centre along the promenade — for those who put peace first.

items.name: Amara
items.description: The modern district next to the train and bus stations: prices a notch friendlier, the centre within walking distance. A sensible base for a Basque tour.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: On the green Atlantic coast the weather is a lottery, but the city is delicious in every season: September means film, January drums, summer the beach.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The Green Season
items.subtitle: Spring · Days of rain breaks and terraces
items.description: The hills are lush green and beach walks cool and lively; rain can visit at any moment. The last of the cider season spills into April — the terraces open at full strength in June.

callout.label: April tip
callout.text: Go to a sagardotegi before cider season ends (Jan-Apr): walk to the barrel at the cry of 'txotx!', hold your glass at an angle, and complete the ritual of cod omelette and txuleta. The villages half an hour from town were built for exactly this.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Beach and Festival
items.subtitle: Summer · La Concha full, the sky festive
items.description: The city switches to beach mode: La Concha blooms with umbrellas, in July the jazz festival turns the beaches into stages, and mid-August is crowned by Semana Grande's fireworks competition. Prices and occupancy peak.

callout.label: August note
callout.text: Finding a hotel in Semana Grande week (around 15 August) is a battle — book months ahead. Your reward: fireworks competing over the bay every night, a world-class show watched from the beach.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Film and Harvest
items.subtitle: Autumn · Festival red carpet, a warm sea
items.description: September is the city's star month: the film festival rolls out the red carpet, the sea is still swimmable, the light is photographer's light. October and November are quiet — the window for the flavour-and-walking traveller.

callout.label: September tip
callout.text: In film festival week, star-spotting around the Kursaal is fair game, but the real pleasure is elsewhere: screening tickets are sold to the public at surprisingly fair prices — landing in a world premiere is luck, Donostia-style.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Drums and Storms
items.subtitle: Winter · Tamborrada, wave shows, cider opening
items.description: Winter is mild but stormy: the waves perform on the Paseo Nuevo and the bars are snug. On 20 January the city drums for 24 hours straight — the Tamborrada is one of the world's loudest and most joyful town festivals.

callout.label: 20 January tip
callout.text: Tamborrada night begins at midnight on the 19th in Konstituzio Plaza: the whole city drums until morning. Don't plan on sleeping — prepare your ears and your stomach's cider capacity.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: In this city 'what to eat' means 'where to begin': counter classics, hot lists and century-old rituals — all within walking distance.

local_word.definition: The legend considered the first pintxo: anchovy, olive and guindilla pepper on a toothpick. Named after Rita Hayworth's film — described as 'salty, green and a little spicy'. This is every crawl's opening move.

items.name: Open with a gilda
items.description: The toothpick trio: anchovy, olive, guindilla. A glass of txakoli alongside — the crawl's official starting whistle. The salt-sour-heat balance primes the palate for the journey.
items.tag: At the first bar · with txakoli

items.name: The tortilla watch
items.description: Some bars' potato omelette hits the counter twice a day and vanishes in minutes: molten centre, caramelised onion. Ask the coming-out time and join the vigil — in this city, tortilla is serious business.
items.tag: At the coming-out hour · molten centre

items.name: Txuleta — the Basque steak
items.description: From mature cattle, thick-cut, seared over coals and crimson inside: the summit of Basque beef culture. Found at every scale from pintxo to full portion — if you don't like it rare, say so at the start.
items.tag: Over coals · rare is the tradition

items.name: The mastery of anchovy and cod
items.description: Cantabrian anchovy on buttered toast, cod (bakalao) in pil-pil sauce: the coast's two prides. Stretch towards Getaria and the legend of coal-grilled turbot (rodaballo) awaits.

items.name: The La Viña-style cheesecake
items.description: The burnt-outside, creamy-inside Basque cheesecake was born in this city's old quarter and conquered the world: eat the original where it began, at room temperature. A sweet sherry is the classic escort.
items.tag: Where it was born · at room temperature

items.name: Cider and the txotx ritual
items.description: At the sagardotegi the barrel is opened, you queue at the cry of 'txotx!', the glass held at an angle: the cider makes its foam in mid-air. In the January-April season the menu is fixed — omelette, cod, txuleta, walnuts.

callout.label: Crawl strategy
callout.text: The pintxo crawl has three rules: one speciality per bar, small drinks (a zurito of beer, a txikito of wine), a route of at least four bars. Don't settle for the cold counter — whoever orders from the hot list plays in the division above.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees La Concha; these six are Donostia's backstage.

items.name: Peine del Viento
items.description: Chillida's 'Comb of the Wind' sculptures are driven into the rocks at Ondarreta's end: in a storm the blowholes beneath them huff like an organ and waves burst over the stone. The point where the city married art to nature.

items.rarity: An island beach in the bay
items.name: Santa Clara island
items.description: A boat service runs in summer to the little island in the bay's middle: a mini beach, an island bar and a reverse angle on La Concha. If you're ambitious, swim there — the locals' summer classic.

items.name: The Paseo Nuevo loop
items.description: The sea-level corniche circling Urgull: meditation on calm days, wave theatre in a storm. Watching big surf without a soaking takes skill — start from the aquarium corner.

items.rarity: A time capsule on the hill
items.name: The Monte Igueldo funfair
items.description: The hilltop funfair from 1912: the wooden 'Swiss mountain' railway curls along the cliff edge with La Concha stretched below. One of the world's most graceful pairings of nostalgia and view.

items.name: The Bretxa market stalls
items.description: In the old town's market, fishmongers and butchers trade shoulder to shoulder with chefs: anchovy fillets, idiazabal cheese and the season's mushrooms. The raw material of the pintxos is chosen here.

items.rarity: Surf culture at the river mouth
items.name: Zurriola at sunset
items.description: Gros's beach fills with surfer silhouettes in the late afternoon: behind the waves, the Kursaal cubes glow. Come without a towel, lean on the railing — watch the city's youngest hour.

callout.label: The order of the views
callout.text: Don't stack the three viewpoints into one day: save Urgull for sunset, Igueldo for the morning and the Peine del Viento for a stormy or big-swell hour. The same bay shows three entirely different cities.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Donostia is an honest city of flavour; its traps are few, but they shadow the crawl of the unprepared.

items.name: Sitting down in one bar and eating a menu
items.description: The visitor sees the first counter, takes a table and fills up: the city's real game — the bar-by-bar speciality hunt — never begins.
items.instead: Stay standing: one pintxo + one small drink per bar, then walk. A crowded bar with napkins on the floor is a good sign; an empty bar before 1 pm is normal, in the evening it's a warning.

items.name: Taking from the counter and not counting
items.description: The open counter runs on trust: at the exit you're asked how many pintxos you had. Whoever forgets to count — or thinks 'they didn't see' — spoils the system's pleasure for everyone.
items.instead: Keep track and declare honestly at the exit; if unsure, stack your plates. Hot orders go on a tab anyway — no confusion there.

items.name: The walk-in Michelin dream
items.description: The city's starred tables fill months ahead; the dream of walking in leaves your evening without a plan.
items.instead: If a star is the goal, book months out; if not, don't grieve — this city's counter gastronomy beats most countries' starred menus. Lunch menus are the fair-priced back door into starred kitchens.

items.name: Arriving unplanned in August
items.description: Semana Grande and beach season pile on top of each other: hotels full, prices at the peak, La Concha towel to towel.
items.instead: If August is unavoidable, lock in lodging early and become a morning beach person; if you're flexible, choose September — the same sea, half the density, festival light as a bonus.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Donostia you don't need to hunt for good food — finding bad food is the hard part; still, let your compass be: a local crowd, napkins on the floor and a handwritten hot list on the wall. Where all three meet, walk in blind.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: A full dose of Donostia, from bay to counter

steps.title: The La Concha paseo
steps.description: A morning walk on the white-balustraded promenade: the bay calm, the light soft. Enter the old town past the city hall and drink your coffee on the square.

steps.title: The Urgull climb
steps.description: Up the path on the hill behind the old town: ramparts, the statue and the bay from above. Descend by the Paseo Nuevo corniche — the waves keep you company.

steps.title: The first pintxo crawl
steps.description: Open with a gilda, join the tortilla watch, order a gem from the hot list: three bars, three specialities, a zurito and a txakoli alongside.

steps.title: Ondarreta and the Peine del Viento
steps.description: Walk the promenade to the bay's far end: watch the conversation of wave and iron at Chillida's wind comb. A beach break on the way back is allowed.

steps.title: The Igueldo funicular
steps.description: Up in the wooden carriage: La Concha's postcard angle and the century-old funfair. As the sunset light turns the bay to gold, you're above it.

steps.title: The evening crawl and a cheesecake finale
steps.description: A second pintxo round: txuleta and anchovy this time. Close in the old quarter with burnt cheesecake + sweet sherry — a Donostia day is sealed like this.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: City, waves and the Basque coast

steps.title: Classic Donostia
steps.description: The one-day flow above: promenade, Urgull, pintxo crawls, Igueldo, cheesecake.

steps.title: Gros and deeper flavour
steps.description: A surf lesson or beach morning at Zurriola; modern pintxos in Gros's young bars at noon; in the evening either a starred reservation or the sagardotegi ritual (if in season) — both extremes are legitimate.

steps.title: A Basque coast escape
steps.description: Getaria in the morning: the fishing port and coal-grilled turbot; the Zarautz shore or Hondarribia's coloured old town in the afternoon; one last gilda on return — the farewell is tradition.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Spanish works everywhere, but three words of Basque open smiles on the counter's far side.

items.meaning: Hello (Basque) — say it entering the bar; it makes a difference
Thank you very much (Basque) — long, but the effect is guaranteed
Please — the Spanish works everywhere, the Basque is a gesture
Cheers! (Basque) — as the txakoli glass rises
Goodbye (Basque) — said on the way out; it closes the door beautifully

checklist.title: San Sebastián Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Topa! You've done the pintxo capital properly!

items.sub: One speciality per bar — no sitting

items.label: Catch a tortilla coming out
items.sub: Ask the hour; it vanishes in minutes

items.sub: Along the white balustrade, late afternoon

items.sub: A free climb, gold at sunset

Listen to the waves at the Peine del Viento
